title: Primitive types: string, number, boolean
hook: TypeScript's three everyday primitives — `string`, `number`, and `boolean` — describe the same JavaScript values you already use. The difference is the compiler checks your intent before the code ships.

blocks.text: **Primitive types** are the simplest building blocks in TypeScript's type system. `string` holds text, `number` holds all numeric values (integers and decimals), and `boolean` holds `true` or `false`. At run time these are ordinary JavaScript values — TypeScript adds compile-time checking only. There is no separate `int`, `float`, or `decimal` like C#; every numeric literal is typed as `number` (IEEE 754 double-precision floating point).

entries.plainDefinition: A sequence of characters. Immutable — concatenation creates a new string.
All JavaScript numbers — integers, decimals, and special values like `Infinity` and `NaN` (Not a Number).
A logical flag. Not convertible to 0/1 like C.
A separate primitive for integers larger than `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`. Suffix literals with `n`.

blocks.text: Choosing and annotating primitives correctly prevents silent bugs. Passing a string where a number is expected fails at compile time instead of at run time. Money calculations need extra care: `number` shares the same `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` surprise as JavaScript — there is no built-in `decimal` type like C#. For currency, many teams store integer cents or use a library.

blocks.title: Quick picker
blocks.body: Text and URLs → `string`. Counters, indexes, prices (with care) → `number`. Flags and conditions → `boolean`. IDs beyond 2^53 − 1 → `bigint`.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Explicit annotation
items.body: Write the type after the variable name: `let count: number = 0;`. Use when the initializer is missing or the type is wider than the value.

items.title: Type inference
items.body: When you assign immediately, TypeScript infers the type: `const name = "Ada"` → `string`. `const` literals narrow to the exact value (see literal types topic).

items.title: Widening on let
items.body: `let x = "hello"` widens to `string`, not the literal `"hello"`. Use `const` or `as const` when you need a fixed literal type.

items.title: Remember: one number type
items.body: Unlike C#'s `int`, `long`, `double`, and `decimal`, TypeScript has a single `number`. Pick libraries or integer cents for exact money math.

snippet.label: Basic primitive annotations
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `string` for URLs and text. Line 2: `let` allows reassignment within the `number` type. Line 3: `const` locks the binding but the type is still `boolean`. Line 6: assigning a string to `number` is rejected at compile time.

snippet.label: number imprecision — same as JavaScript
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–3: binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly — identical to JavaScript and C# `double`. Lines 5–6: a common pattern for money is integer cents to avoid rounding surprises. Interview answer: TypeScript has no `decimal`; use cents or a decimal library.

snippet.label: bigint for large integer IDs
snippet.explanation: Line 1: beyond this value, `number` loses integer precision. Line 2: `bigint` handles arbitrary-size integers with the `n` suffix. Lines 5–6: `number` and `bigint` are separate types — convert explicitly before arithmetic.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `number` for currency without mentioning rounding risk. Assuming TypeScript has `int` or `decimal` like C#. Comparing `bigint` and `number` without conversion. Forgetting that `typeof null === "object"` in JavaScript (TypeScript still types `null` separately).

blocks.text: TypeScript primitives are erased at emit — `string` becomes plain JavaScript string with no run-time tag. `number` is always IEEE 754 double; there is no separate float/int at the type level. For Redis TTL math or fee calculations, senior engineers document whether they accept floating-point drift or use integer cents. `bigint` cannot be JSON-serialized natively — plan conversions at API boundaries.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Assuming immutability prevents new allocation on concat
Using for money without cents or decimal lib
Truthy coercion still happens at run time

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming TypeScript has a decimal type. Saying primitives are boxed at run time like C# value types. Ignoring 0.1 + 0.2 when discussing financial calculations.

interviewTakeaways: TypeScript has string, number, boolean, bigint — number is always IEEE 754 double.
No built-in decimal — use integer cents or a library for money.
Types are compile-time only; erased when emitting JavaScript.
60s: string for text. number is double like JS. boolean for flags. bigint for huge ints. No decimal primitive.
Follow-up: how would you model currency without floating-point error?
commonPitfalls: Using number for money without mentioning rounding — weak answer.
Claiming TypeScript has int/long/decimal like C#.
Strong answer: 'number is IEEE 754 double. For money use cents or decimal.js. bigint for IDs beyond MAX_SAFE_INTEGER.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript `typeof` returns "string", "number", "boolean", "bigint". TypeScript adds static checking on top of the same run-time values.
C# splits numerics into int, long, double, decimal. TypeScript collapses them into `number` (double). See basic-types-vs-csharp topic.
